The narrator murdered their spouse, then forged a farewell note in the spouse's handwriting to make it appear the spouse had left voluntarily—ending with "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back." To imitate the spouse's writing, the narrator repeatedly rehearsed the key line ("You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back."), producing seven practice copies. Those seven practice lines survive as damning evidence of the forgery, so when the narrator sighs "I know I'm in trouble," they recognize that the handwriting practice will expose the murder and the fake note.

The narrator murdered their spouse, then tried to make it seem the spouse had left voluntarily by forging a farewell note reading "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back." To imitate the spouse's handwriting, the narrator rehearsed that line repeatedly, producing seven practice copies. The seven repetitions themselves are the damning evidence: they show the narrator deliberately rehearsing the exact phrase used in the fake note, exposing the forgery and thus the murder. The closing "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble" is the narrator realizing that this handwriting practice will reveal what they did.
